title: Pillar II — Next.js & Server Component Architectures

sections.heading: Where does the HTML come from?
paragraphs: Every rendering strategy answers one question: where and when is the HTML produced? CSR: in the browser, after a JS bundle loads. SSR: on the server, per request. SSG: on the server, once at build time. ISR: SSG plus scheduled regeneration.

Next.js lets you choose per route. A marketing page wants SSG (fast, cacheable, content rarely changes). A personalized dashboard wants SSR or client fetching (data differs per user, per request). A product catalog updated hourly is the ISR sweet spot.
The trade axis is freshness versus latency versus server cost. Memorize the axis, not a table — interviewers reward reasoning from constraints.
sections.summary: Pick a rendering strategy by asking how fresh the content must be, whether it differs per user, and how much traffic it gets.

variants.question: A news site's article pages must reflect edits within about a minute, get heavy traffic, and are identical for every visitor. Which strategy fits best?
options: Pure CSR — fetch the article JSON in the browser per view
SSR that re-renders the identical page on every request
SSG with ISR, revalidating roughly every 60 seconds
Static export rebuilt by hand when an editor remembers
variants.rationale: Identical-for-everyone content is the static sweet spot, and ISR's revalidation window handles 'fresh within a minute' without paying a server render per request. Heavy traffic hits cached static HTML; regeneration happens at most once per window.
optionExplanations: CSR gives crawlers and first paint an empty shell and pays a fetch on every view — worst of all worlds for public content pages.
SSR works but renders the same identical page thousands of times per minute — pure wasted compute versus caching it.
Correct — static delivery with automatic freshness is exactly what ISR was built for.
Manual rebuilds violate the one-minute freshness requirement the moment a human forgets.
variants.interviewTip: Frame rendering-strategy answers around three questions: Is the content per-user? How fresh must it be? What's the traffic? The strategy falls out of the answers.

variants.question: A logged-in banking dashboard shows each user's own account balances and recent transactions, which must be accurate the instant the page loads. Traffic is moderate. Which rendering strategy fits best?
options: A single static export regenerated nightly by a scheduled cron job
SSG built once at build time and shared across every logged-in user
SSG with ISR revalidating the shared page every 30 seconds on a timer
SSR per request (or a per-user client fetch) using live data
variants.rationale: The content is per-user and must be exact on load, so there is nothing to safely cache and share. Rendering per request (SSR) — or fetching that user's data client-side after auth — is the only approach that guarantees each visitor sees their own live balances.
optionExplanations: A nightly-regenerated static file is both shared across users and stale by up to a day — doubly disqualifying for live per-user finances.
Build-time SSG produces one HTML file for everyone, which cannot represent per-user balances and would leak or misreport data.
ISR still caches and shares a single generated page across users within the window — wrong for anything personalized and potentially a data-leak.
Correct — per-user, must-be-live data is the canonical case for SSR or authenticated client fetching rather than any shared cache.
variants.interviewTip: The single fastest disqualifier for any caching strategy is 'is this per-user?' If yes, shared static/ISR output is off the table before you even discuss freshness.

variants.question: An internal ops dashboard sits behind SSO, serves about 40 employees, and displays near-real-time queue metrics that the UI re-polls every few seconds. SEO is irrelevant. Which rendering approach is the most defensible?
options: SSG with ISR so the metrics page regenerates on a fixed timed schedule
CSR — an authenticated shell that polls the metrics API in the browser
SSR on every request so the first paint always carries fresh numbers
A static export that CI rebuilds whenever the queue metrics change
variants.rationale: This is the scenario where CSR is the honest answer: no SEO to serve, a tiny authenticated audience, and data that updates continuously within a session. The polling loop means the page's real freshness comes from client fetches regardless of how the first paint was produced, so paying for server rendering or shared caching buys almost nothing.
optionExplanations: ISR shares one cached page across users on a timer — pointless when the client immediately re-polls, and a shared cache is the wrong shape for an authenticated internal tool.
Correct — when SEO doesn't matter and the data is refreshed in-session by polling, client-side fetching is the right tool; reflexively rejecting CSR is itself the interview trap.
SSR's fresh first paint is stale within seconds once the polling loop takes over — you pay a server render per request for a head start that evaporates immediately.
Metrics changing every few seconds would mean CI rebuilding continuously — a build pipeline cannot be your realtime data path.
variants.interviewTip: Show you can argue *for* CSR, not just against it: no SEO requirement, authenticated audience, and continuously polled data are the three flags that make client-side fetching the defensible pick.

variants.question: Your terms-of-service and privacy pages change maybe three times a year — always through a reviewed code deploy — are identical for every visitor, and serve a global audience. A teammate proposes ISR with `revalidate: 60` 'to be safe.' What do you recommend?
options: Accept it — a short ISR window is the safest default for any public page
SSR, because legal content is too important to ever serve from a cache
CSR, so the legal team can swap the text without an engineering deploy
Plain build-time SSG — deploys rebuild the page, so ISR just adds cost
variants.rationale: The freshness requirement is coupled to deploys: the only event that changes the content is a rebuild, which republishes the static page by definition. ISR here schedules background regenerations that can never observe a change between deploys — pure waste. Reasoning from the cause of change rather than defaulting to 'add revalidation' is what the question tests.
optionExplanations: A 60-second window on content that changes three times a year triggers thousands of no-op regenerations — 'safe' here just means 'wasteful'.
Per-request rendering of a page that is byte-identical for everyone and changes triannually is the least efficient option on the board.
CSR sacrifices instant first paint and crawler-friendly HTML on the pages where trust and indexability matter, to solve a publishing-workflow problem that doesn't exist.
Correct — when content changes only via deploys, build-time SSG is already perfectly fresh; ISR would be solving a staleness problem the architecture cannot have.
variants.interviewTip: Ask 'what event changes this content?' If the answer is 'a deploy', build-time SSG is complete on its own — proposing ISR anyway signals cargo-culting rather than reasoning.

sections.heading: Hydration — and how it breaks
paragraphs: Server-rendered HTML is a lifeless picture. Hydration is React running in the browser, re-rendering the same tree, and attaching listeners and state to the existing markup instead of rebuilding it.

The contract: the client's first render must produce the same output as the server's. Anything that differs between the two environments breaks it — `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, locale-dependent formatting, or reading `window` at render time.

That last one has an extra sting: `window` doesn't exist in Node at all, so a top-scope or render-time `window` reference doesn't just mismatch — it throws `window is not defined` during the server render and can take the whole route down.
sections.summary: The server and browser must first render the same thing, so keep time, randomness, and `window` out of that first render.

variants.question: A component renders `{new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}`. In Next.js it triggers a hydration mismatch warning. What's the root cause?
options: Server and client render the time at different moments — two outputs
Dates in React must always be wrapped inside a useEffect hook to render
A span element is simply not allowed to contain any dynamic text at all
The toLocaleTimeString method is not available in the Node.js runtime
variants.rationale: Hydration compares server HTML against the client's first render. A wall-clock timestamp is different on every call — and locale/timezone can differ between server and browser too. Fix: render a stable placeholder, then set the time in useEffect (client-only, post-hydration), or pass a fixed server timestamp as a prop.
optionExplanations: Correct — nondeterministic output between the server pass and client pass is the definition of a hydration mismatch.
Not all dates — a stable date passed as a prop renders identically in both passes. The rule targets nondeterminism, not the Date type.
Spans hold dynamic text constantly; the element is irrelevant.
Node implements toLocaleTimeString fine; the function runs — it just returns a different value than the client's run.
variants.interviewTip: Give the general law, not the instance: 'anything nondeterministic or environment-dependent — time, random, window, locale — must move out of the initial render, usually into useEffect.'

variants.question: A component reads `const width = window.innerWidth` at the top of its render body to pick a layout. Locally it looks fine, but a production build crashes the route with `window is not defined` before any HTML is even sent. Why — and how does this differ from a normal hydration mismatch?
options: It's just an ordinary hydration mismatch; wrapping the whole JSX in a `<Suspense>` boundary quietly silences the warning
`window` doesn't exist in the Node server render, so reading it throws and no HTML comes out — a crash, not a warning
`innerWidth` is a reserved DOM property name that Next.js forbids any component from reading during its render body
The build fails only because `window` must first be imported from the `next/navigation` module before it can be used
variants.rationale: Server Components (and the SSR pass of Client Components) run in Node, where `window` simply does not exist. A render-time `window` access throws `ReferenceError` during the server render, so the route errors out before emitting HTML. That is strictly worse than a hydration mismatch, which still renders something and only warns about a difference. The fix is to read `window` only after mount — in a `useEffect` or behind a `typeof window !== 'undefined'` guard in a Client Component.
optionExplanations: A Suspense boundary handles pending async work, not synchronous ReferenceErrors thrown at render time; the server render still crashes.
Correct — the browser global is absent in Node, so the reference throws during SSR and prevents any HTML from being produced, unlike a mismatch that renders then warns.
`innerWidth` is a perfectly ordinary DOM property; nothing about its name is special or forbidden.
`window` is a browser global, not an export of `next/navigation`; importing from there does nothing to make it exist on the server.
variants.interviewTip: Distinguish the two failure modes out loud: nondeterministic-but-present values (time, random) cause hydration mismatch warnings; browser-only globals (`window`, `document`, `localStorage`) throw server-side and can take the whole route down. The second is more severe.

variants.question: A landing page picks its hero image with `const hero = heroes[Math.floor(Math.random() * heroes.length)]` in the render body. The page loads and displays, but the console logs a hydration error and the hero occasionally flickers to a different image right after load. What is actually happening?
options: `Math.random()` is seeded differently in Node — a known Next.js bug that upgrading React fixes
The image failed to preload, so a Suspense boundary quietly swapped in its fallback element instead
Server and client rolled different random indices; React warned, then patched the DOM to the client's
Random array indices break React's key-based reconciliation; adding a `key` prop to the `` fixes it
variants.rationale: `Math.random()` is nondeterministic, so the server pass and the client's first render disagree — the textbook hydration mismatch. Crucially, the page still renders: mismatches warn and patch rather than crash. Fixes: choose the variant once on the server and pass it down as a prop, derive it deterministically from a seed, or select it post-mount in `useEffect`.
optionExplanations: Node's `Math.random()` works fine and no upgrade changes this — the problem is calling any nondeterministic function during a render that must be reproducible across environments.
Suspense fallbacks relate to pending async work, not `` loading, and swapping a fallback wouldn't produce a hydration warning in the console.

Correct — two independent random rolls across the server and client passes violate the hydration contract; React reconciles by overwriting with the client's roll, which the user perceives as a flicker.
Keys govern list identity across re-renders; they do nothing about the server and client disagreeing on what to render in the first place.
variants.interviewTip: Name the contract, then the severity: nondeterministic values (random, time) break hydration but still render — a warning plus a DOM patch. Contrast that with browser-only globals, which crash the server render outright.

variants.question: To restore a saved theme, a Client Component runs `const theme = localStorage.getItem('theme') ?? 'light'` directly in its render body. The route errors server-side with `localStorage is not defined`. A teammate is confused: 'it has `'use client'` — why is it running on the server at all?' What's the correct diagnosis and fix?
options: `'use client'` still server-renders to HTML in Node, where `localStorage` is absent — read it in `useEffect` after mount
The teammate is right that Client Components never run on the server, so the error must come from a Server Component elsewhere
Next.js blocks `localStorage` for security reasons; the only supported storage API is cookies read through `next/headers`
Wrap the whole component in a `<Suspense>` boundary so the server defers it and only the browser ever renders that subtree
variants.rationale: The misconception under test: `'use client'` does not mean 'renders only in the browser'. Client Components are still server-rendered to HTML for the initial response, and that pass runs in Node where `localStorage`, `window`, and `document` don't exist. Browser-only APIs must wait until after mount — read the stored theme in `useEffect` (accepting a brief default-theme paint), or move the preference into a cookie the server can read.
optionExplanations: Correct — the SSR pass of a Client Component runs in Node, so render-time `localStorage` access throws; a post-mount `useEffect` is the standard home for browser storage reads.
This is precisely the misconception the bug exposes — Client Components absolutely do execute on the server to produce the initial HTML.
There is no such security block; `localStorage` simply doesn't exist in Node. Cookies are a legitimate alternative design, but the stated reasoning is wrong.
Suspense coordinates async rendering; it doesn't exempt a component from the server pass or catch a synchronous `ReferenceError` thrown during it.
variants.interviewTip: Repeat the sharpest line in the App Router: `'use client'` means 'ships JavaScript to the browser', not 'skips the server'. Interviewers plant this exact confusion to see whether you correct it.

sections.heading: Server Components vs Client Components
paragraphs: In the App Router, components are Server Components by default: they run only on the server, can query a database or read files directly, and ship zero JavaScript to the browser. Their code never reaches the client bundle.

Adding `'use client'` marks a component (and everything it imports) as a Client Component — it still gets server-rendered to HTML, but its code ships to the browser and hydrates. You need it for state, effects, event handlers, and browser APIs.

The composition rule: server can render client, but a Client Component cannot import a Server Component. It can, however, receive one as `children` — which is how you keep an interactive shell from dragging the whole subtree into the client bundle.
sections.summary: Components run on the server by default; add `'use client'` only where you truly need clicks, state, or browser features.

variants.question: Which of these forces a component to be a Client Component in the App Router?
options: Fetching remote data with async and await in the body
Rendering a list of items with the array .map() method
Using useState together with an onClick event handler
Importing a plain CSS stylesheet file into the module
variants.rationale: Interactivity is the dividing line. State, effects, event handlers, and browser APIs require JavaScript running in the browser — that's what 'use client' opts into. Data fetching, mapping, and styling all work fine (often better) on the server.
optionExplanations: Server Components are the *preferred* place for async data fetching — an async component that awaits a query is the flagship pattern.
.map() is plain rendering logic, equally at home in either world.
Correct — state and event handlers only exist in the browser, so they demand a Client Component.
CSS imports work in Server Components; styles don't need client-side JS.
variants.interviewTip: A sharp line interviewers love: ''use client' doesn't mean renders on the client — it still SSRs. It means ships JavaScript to the client.'

variants.question: You have a Client Component `<Sidebar>` (it uses `useState` for a collapse toggle). You want to render a data-heavy `<Feed>` Server Component — which queries the database directly — inside that sidebar's layout without turning `<Feed>` into client code. What is the correct composition?
options: Move the database query into `<Sidebar>` and pass the raw fetched rows down to `<Feed>` as props
Add a `'use client'` directive to `<Feed>` so it is allowed to sit inside `<Sidebar>`'s tree
Have `<Sidebar>` directly `import Feed from './feed'` and render `<Feed />` inside its own JSX
In a Server Component parent, render `<Feed>` and pass it to `<Sidebar>` as `children`
variants.rationale: A Client Component cannot import a Server Component (importing it pulls it into the client bundle and forces it client-side). But a Client Component can receive an already-rendered Server Component through `children` or a prop. So a server parent renders `<Feed>` and hands it to `<Sidebar>` — `<Feed>` stays server-only and never ships to the browser.
optionExplanations: Moving the DB query into a Client Component means running database access in code destined for the browser — impossible and a security hazard; the whole point was to keep `<Feed>` on the server.
Marking `<Feed>` as a Client Component defeats the goal: it can no longer query the database directly and its code now ships to the client.
A Client Component importing a Server Component is exactly the forbidden pattern — it drags `<Feed>` into the client bundle and forces it to run client-side.
Correct — the children/slot pattern lets a server-rendered subtree be passed through an interactive client shell without the shell importing it.
variants.interviewTip: State the rule and its escape hatch together: 'A Client Component can't import a Server Component, but it can accept one as children.' Naming the children-as-slot pattern signals you've actually shipped App Router code.

variants.question: A page section must call a third-party API using a secret key that can never reach the browser. Where does that call belong in the App Router, and why?
options: In a Client Component's `useEffect`, reading the key from `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_KEY` and calling the API
Anywhere at all — Next.js automatically strips every environment variable out of client bundles, so placement is irrelevant
In a Client Component, but with the secret key obfuscated first before it gets embedded in the shipped JS bundle
In a Server Component — its code and non-public env vars never ship to the browser, so the key stays server-side
variants.rationale: Server Components run exclusively on the server and their code is never part of the client bundle, which makes them the structural answer to secret handling: the key isn't hidden, it simply never travels. The `NEXT_PUBLIC_` option is the planted trap — that prefix explicitly opts a variable *into* the client bundle, the exact opposite of what a secret needs.
optionExplanations: `NEXT_PUBLIC_` is the escape hatch that inlines a variable into browser-delivered JavaScript — using it for a secret publishes the secret.
Non-public vars are indeed absent from client bundles, but that means a Client Component reading one just gets `undefined` — placement decides access, so 'anywhere' is exactly wrong.
Anything embedded in a client bundle is readable by anyone who opens DevTools; obfuscating shipped code is not a security boundary.
Correct — server-only execution means the key and the code using it never leave the server; this is the flagship security argument for Server Components.
variants.interviewTip: Frame secrets as a shipping problem, not a hiding problem: the only key that can't leak from the browser is one that was never sent there. Then name-drop the `server-only` package to show you know how to enforce the boundary at build time.

variants.question: To fix a single `<LikeButton>` that needs `onClick`, a teammate adds `'use client'` at the top of the entire `DashboardPage` file — which also imports a chart library, a data table, and a `db.ts` query helper. It appears to work in dev. What is the real cost of that directive's placement?
options: None at all — `'use client'` is merely an advisory annotation that doesn't change what actually gets bundled for the browser
It makes the module and imports client code: charts and table ship to the browser and `db` access breaks — scope to a leaf
The whole page stops being server-rendered entirely from that point on, so its search-engine SEO is completely destroyed
Bundle size is left unaffected because Next.js automatically tree-shakes all server-only imports back out of client files
variants.rationale: `'use client'` marks a boundary, and everything imported past that boundary becomes client code. Hoisting it to a page-level file drags heavy visualization libraries into the browser bundle and pulls database-touching code toward the client, where it either fails to build or leaks connection details. The discipline is to push the directive down to the smallest leaf that actually needs interactivity.
optionExplanations: The directive materially changes module classification and bundling — it is one of the most consequential single lines you can add to a file.
Correct — client-ness is contagious through the import graph from the directive downward; scoping it to the smallest interactive leaf is the core App Router bundle discipline.
Client Components are still server-rendered to HTML on first load — SEO is not the casualty here; bundle size and server-only access are.
No such tree-shaking exists for this case — imports of a client module become client code, which is exactly why the directive's placement matters.
variants.interviewTip: Say 'push `'use client'` to the leaves' and explain why: the directive defines a boundary and everything it imports crosses to the client side of it. This question separates people who've read the docs from people who've watched their bundle analyzer.

sections.heading: Data fetching and caching in the App Router
paragraphs: In Server Components you fetch where you render: `const data = await db.query(...)` right inside the async component. No useEffect-plus-loading-spinner dance, no API round-trip from the browser for the initial view.

Next.js layers caching on top: fetch results can be cached and tagged, routes can be static or dynamic, and `revalidatePath`/`revalidateTag` let a mutation surgically invalidate exactly the cached data it changed.

Server Actions close the write loop: a function marked `'use server'` can be passed to a form's `action`, runs on the server when submitted, mutates data, and revalidates — often with zero hand-written API endpoints.
sections.summary: Fetch data right inside server components, and after a change, tell Next.js exactly what to refresh instead of guessing on a timer.

variants.question: After a Server Action creates a new post, the posts list page still shows the old list. What's the idiomatic App Router fix?
options: Call revalidatePath('/posts') inside the action after the write
Set every fetch to cache: 'no-store' across the whole application
Store the posts list in localStorage and update that copy by hand
Call router.refresh() inside a setInterval so the page keeps polling
variants.rationale: The list is stale because it was served from the cache. The action just changed that data, so the action is the right place to declare it: revalidatePath/revalidateTag invalidates precisely the affected cache entries, and the next render is fresh — no polling, no global cache surrender.
optionExplanations: Correct — mutate, then revalidate the paths/tags that depend on the mutated data.
Disabling caching app-wide fixes one stale list by making every page slower forever — a sledgehammer with collateral damage.
localStorage creates a second source of truth on one device; the server and every other client still disagree.
Polling burns requests to discover a change your own code just made — you already know the exact moment the data changed.
variants.interviewTip: The pattern to articulate: 'mutations own their invalidations' — whoever writes the data revalidates the caches that read it.

variants.question: One product's price is fetched with `fetch(url, { next: { tags: ['product-42'] } })` and cached across several pages (the product page, the homepage carousel, the search index). An admin edits that one product's price. You want the edit to refresh every page showing product 42 — but leave the thousands of other cached products untouched. What's the most precise mechanism?
options: Call `revalidatePath('/')` so the entire site re-renders and eventually picks up the price change
Call `revalidateTag('product-42')` in the mutation to invalidate exactly its entries
Set `cache: 'no-store'` on the product fetch so that it is simply never cached in the first place
Call `router.refresh()` on the client right after the admin saves the edited product price
variants.rationale: Because the fetch was tagged `product-42`, every cached entry that used it — across all pages — is bound to that tag. `revalidateTag('product-42')` invalidates precisely those entries and nothing else, so the one product refreshes everywhere it appears while the rest of the cache stays warm. Tags are the tool for 'one piece of data appears on many routes.'
optionExplanations: `revalidatePath('/')` is far broader than needed — it dumps the homepage's entire cache (and misses other routes showing the product unless you revalidate each), the opposite of surgical.
Correct — tag-based revalidation targets exactly the cache entries that read this datum, regardless of which routes they live on, leaving unrelated products cached.
`no-store` throws away caching for that product permanently, paying a fresh fetch on every view forever to solve a problem that only occurs at edit time.
`router.refresh()` re-fetches on one client's session and doesn't invalidate the shared server cache other visitors are served from.
variants.interviewTip: Contrast the two knobs: `revalidatePath` targets a route, `revalidateTag` targets a piece of data wherever it appears. When the same datum is cached across many routes, tags are the precise instrument.

variants.question: You're building a 'create comment' feature. A teammate starts scaffolding `app/api/comments/route.ts` plus a client-side `fetch` POST with hand-rolled loading state. What's the idiomatic App Router alternative, and what does it buy you?
options: There isn't one — Route Handlers are genuinely the only sanctioned way to mutate data from any of your forms in Next.js
A GET Route Handler that performs the database insert whenever the form navigates the browser to its URL
A `'use server'` Server Action on the form's `action`: it runs on submit, colocates the mutation, and revalidates
Marking the client fetch `cache: 'no-store'` so that the POST request bypasses the Router Cache entirely
variants.rationale: Server Actions exist precisely to close this loop without a hand-written endpoint: the mutation is a plain function marked `'use server'`, wired straight to the form. You delete the endpoint boilerplate, the client fetch, and the serialization glue — and because the action runs on the server, the write and its cache revalidation live in one place. Progressive enhancement (the form submits even before JS loads) comes free.
optionExplanations: Route Handlers remain useful for external consumers and webhooks, but for your own forms the framework explicitly offers Server Actions as the primary write path.
Mutations over GET violate HTTP semantics and get triggered by prefetching and crawlers — a classic footgun, not an architecture.
Correct — action-on-form is the canonical write path: server execution, colocated revalidation, no bespoke endpoint, and pre-hydration submissions all in one.
`cache: 'no-store'` is a read-caching knob; it has nothing to do with how a mutation is transported or where it runs.
variants.interviewTip: Enumerate what a Server Action deletes from the diff: the endpoint file, the fetch call, the request/response typing, and the loading-state plumbing. Then mention `useActionState`/`useFormStatus` for pending UI to show you've shipped the full pattern.

variants.question: A pricing table uses `export const revalidate = 300`, but prices only change when someone saves them in your internal admin panel — roughly twice a week. Sales complains prices are stale for up to five minutes after each update, and you're paying for regenerations all day. What's the strongest redesign?
options: Move to on-demand invalidation: tag the fetch and have the save mutation call `revalidateTag`, drop the timer
Lower `revalidate` to 10 so the staleness window merely shrinks from five minutes down to about ten seconds
Set the route to `force-dynamic` so that every single visitor always renders fully fresh prices on each request
Have the admin panel append a version query-string onto the pricing URLs so that the stale caches get bypassed
variants.rationale: Time-based revalidation is a guess about when data changes; on-demand revalidation is knowledge. Here the writer is your own code, so the exact moment of change is observable — the save mutation should invalidate the tagged entries, making updates visible immediately while the cache stays warm for the days between edits. The timer was only ever an approximation, and now it can go.
optionExplanations: Correct — when your own system performs the writes, event-driven `revalidateTag` from the mutation gives instant freshness and near-zero wasted regeneration, strictly dominating any interval.
Shrinking the window is a treadmill: staleness never reaches zero and regeneration cost multiplies — you're tuning a guess instead of eliminating it.
`force-dynamic` renders on every request forever to accommodate a change that happens twice a week — maximal cost for a problem with a surgical solution.
Cache-busting query strings fragment your URLs and sidestep the framework's cache rather than invalidating it — the shared server cache still holds the stale entry.
variants.interviewTip: Contrast the two revalidation philosophies: interval-based is 'guess when data changes', on-demand is 'be told when data changes'. Whenever the write path is your own code, choosing the interval anyway is a red flag.

sections.heading: Routing, layouts, and the file system
paragraphs: The App Router maps folders to URLs: `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` handles `/blog/hello-world`, with `params.slug` as the dynamic segment. `page.tsx` is the routable leaf; `layout.tsx` wraps it.

Layouts nest and — critically — persist: navigating between two blog posts re-renders the page, but the surrounding layout (nav bar, sidebar) keeps its DOM and state. State that must survive navigation belongs in a layout.

Special files fill out the contract: `loading.tsx` renders instantly (via Suspense) while the page's data streams in, `error.tsx` is a route-scoped error boundary, and `not-found.tsx` handles missing resources.
sections.summary: Folders become URLs, and anything wrapped in a `layout` keeps its state as you move between pages inside it.

variants.question: A search input lives in the nav bar. Users complain its text clears whenever they click a result and navigate. Where should the nav bar live to fix this?
options: In loading.tsx, which re-renders completely fresh on every single navigation
In each page.tsx so that every individual route fully controls its own nav bar
In a shared layout.tsx, which persists its DOM and state across navigations
In a separate iframe element so that ordinary page navigation can't ever touch it
variants.rationale: Layouts don't remount on navigation between their child routes — that's their defining behavior. A nav bar (with its input state) inside the shared layout survives every page change beneath it.
optionExplanations: loading.tsx is a transient Suspense fallback, visible only while a page loads — the opposite of persistent.
Per-page nav bars remount on every navigation — that's precisely the state-clearing behavior being reported.
Correct — layout persistence is the mechanism for cross-navigation UI state.
An iframe technically works and is technically a crime: separate document, broken styling, accessibility pain.
variants.interviewTip: 'What's the difference between layout and template in the App Router?' — layout persists across navigations, template remounts each time. Knowing both exists marks real App Router experience.

variants.question: A signup wizard needs a fresh CSS mount animation to replay every time the user navigates between its steps, and a per-visit analytics 'step viewed' effect that must fire on each navigation. Placing the wrapper in `layout.tsx` breaks both — the animation plays once and the effect never re-runs. Which file gives the wrapper the remount-on-every-navigation behavior you want?
options: `loading.tsx` — it re-renders freshly on every single route change that the user makes here
`page.tsx` — move the wrapper into each individual step's own page so that it naturally remounts
`layout.tsx` — add a `key` prop to the wrapper to force it to remount on each navigation
`template.tsx` — renders a new instance per navigation, remounting DOM and rerunning effects
variants.rationale: `template.tsx` is the deliberate opposite of `layout.tsx`: where a layout persists its instance across navigations, a template creates a fresh instance on each navigation. That remount replays enter animations and re-runs effects like the analytics 'step viewed' event — exactly the requested behavior — while still wrapping the child routes.
optionExplanations: `loading.tsx` is only a Suspense fallback shown while a page's data loads; it isn't a persistent wrapper for the page content and won't host the wizard shell.
Duplicating the wrapper into every page works crudely but abandons the shared-wrapper structure and repeats markup across steps — `template.tsx` provides remount without the duplication.

You can't attach a navigation-varying `key` to the layout element itself from outside it; layouts are defined to persist, and there's no supported prop that flips that per-navigation — `template.tsx` is the built-in answer.
Correct — `template.tsx` remounts on every navigation, giving fresh DOM (replayed animations) and re-run effects, which is precisely why it exists alongside layout.
variants.interviewTip: When someone needs enter animations or per-navigation effects to replay, reach for `template.tsx`; when they need state to survive navigation, reach for `layout.tsx`. They're a matched pair distinguished solely by remount behavior.

variants.question: A podcast app docks a mini audio player at the bottom of the screen; playback must continue seamlessly while the user browses between episode pages. Where does the player belong, and what mechanism makes it work?
options: In `template.tsx`, so that every navigation constructs a brand-new fresh player instance
In a shared `layout.tsx` — it keeps its DOM across navigations, so the `<audio>` never unmounts
In each episode's `page.tsx`, forwarding the current playback timestamp between routes via `searchParams`
In `loading.tsx`, since that file is rendered during every single route transition the user triggers
variants.rationale: Uninterrupted playback requires the `<audio>` element to never leave the DOM — the moment it unmounts, the browser stops the stream. Layout persistence is exactly that guarantee: navigating among the layout's child routes re-renders pages beneath it while the layout's own instance, DOM, and state are preserved. It's the same mechanism as the classic persistent nav bar, applied to media.
optionExplanations: `template.tsx` remounts per navigation by design — each route change would tear down the audio element mid-stream, the precise failure you're trying to avoid.
Correct — layout persistence keeps the audio element mounted across navigations, which is the only way the browser keeps playing without a gap.
Remount-and-seek via `searchParams` guarantees an audible gap and a re-fetched media stream on every navigation — a simulation of persistence, not the real thing.
`loading.tsx` is a transient Suspense fallback that appears and disappears around page loads — the least stable home imaginable for a live media element.
variants.interviewTip: Media players, WebSocket providers, and video calls are the vivid examples of layout persistence — anything that dies on unmount must live in a layout. Citing one shows you understand the mechanism, not just the nav-bar cliché.

variants.question: A dashboard's `layout.tsx` renders a Client Component sidebar whose expanded/collapsed state lives in `useState`. The user collapses it on `/dashboard/settings`, then navigates to `/dashboard/billing` — both under that layout. What happens to the sidebar, and by what mechanism?
options: It re-expands — client-side navigation reconstructs the entire component tree from the root down each time
It stays collapsed, but only because Next.js quietly snapshots the component state into `sessionStorage` between routes
It stays collapsed — the layout instance is preserved across child-route navigations, so its React state survives
It stays collapsed only if the sidebar is converted into a Server Component, because server output gets cached
variants.rationale: This is layout persistence viewed from the state's perspective: on soft navigation the App Router swaps only the route segments that changed and leaves ancestor layouts mounted. Because the sidebar component never unmounts, its `useState` value simply continues to exist — no storage, no serialization, no framework magic beyond not remounting. If remount-per-navigation were ever desired, that's what `template.tsx` provides.
optionExplanations: Soft navigation is surgical, not total — the router replaces only the changed segments; full-tree reconstruction is the full-page-reload mental model the App Router exists to avoid.
No such storage mechanism exists — the state survives because the component instance was never destroyed, which requires no persistence layer at all.
Correct — a preserved layout instance means preserved React state; the collapse boolean lives on because its owner never unmounted.
Server Components can't hold `useState` at all — interactive state is exclusively a Client Component concern, and caching of server output is unrelated to it.
variants.interviewTip: Explain *why* layout state survives — 'the instance is never unmounted' — rather than just asserting that it does. Following up with 'and `template.tsx` is the opt-out when you want remounting' completes the pair in one breath.
